utterances.text: And you can see there that on the 14th of August, a fire had broken out at the UNCRO warehouse. A fire-fighting team was sent and in fact, a member of the military police actually reported the episode to the police and apparently the fire was put out, material damage insignificant. Now, I'll show you a number of these, I'm not going to go through all of them, but if we could please now look at page 21. Thank you. So in that instance, you'd agree the one that we've just looked at the military police are doing what they are supposed to do; yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, Mr. Cayley, may I ask you one thing. Let's first verify with the witness. When you testified that you never saw someone putting out a fire, a fire brigade, were you referring to burning houses or were you referring to UN facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was referring to burning houses out in the different hamlets and in Knin itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the next one that we're looking at here, if we go to the bottom of the page, this is a burning house in Kaldrma village being reported on the 15th of August of 1995 by Damir Vrkic and you'll see, Mr. Munkelien, that steps were taken, if you look at the 7th column along that an on-site investigation was carried out into what had actually taken place. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. 1

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we could move, please, to page 22?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, I appreciate your efforts to establish what happened, but it strikes me, and I'm speaking for myself but it strikes me that the statement of the witness was about putting out fires at homes and fire brigades. Your first example was aspecific, your second example now is aspecific as well, at least does not directly relate to what the witness said because this does not say anything about efforts to put out the fire. It just says there was a report that there had been a fire. It doesn't say anything about sending someone to extinguish that fire, it just says about -- so therefore, I want you to know that if you put questions to the witness, that doesn't stop the Chamber from thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the difficulty I have always, of course, is time allowed. There are many of these reports, I mean there are specific reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then take the strongest ones where someone is sent to extinguish the fire and preferably not at an UNCRO facility and perhaps where people are still to be saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. The next example does actually cover exactly what you're saying. I didn't want to mislead him by just picking and choosing over a period of time, but I'll do as you suggest, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: 15th of August, you'll see there, can you see that, Mr. Munkelien?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I can see it clearly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: They reported via radio -- I'm sorry, we've gone back -- page 22.

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: 22, okay. They reported via radio communications a fire had broken out in a house near the UNCRO base in the field. So here, we're talking about a house. And you'll see there in the seventh column at 2040 hours, a fire fighting team was sent with the team leader Nevan Pavic, Zadar-Knin PU, the firefighters could not reach the house because of the inaccessibility of the terrain. At 1000, the patrol reported that the fire had burnt itself out. If we could look at another example, please, page 31. Bottom of the page, please. Here, we have a fire broke out in a house in Knin, this is 19th August, 1995 at 1615. "Intervention team sent at 1620 hours, a fireman sent at 1630 hours. Operational officers sent at 1635 hours and they took over the case. Fire localised at 1745 hours." If we could please go to page 36, the 20th of August of 1995. And you will see there a report on a fire, 1225 hours B. Meglic from grad police car reported via US radio communications that a house close to the hospital is on fire. And you will see in the next column, Mr. Munkelien, that at 2235 hours, firefighters informed they localised the fire at 0010 hours. I do have -- I'll ask a question now, Your Honour, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Mr. Cayley, as far as time is concerned, I have here apparently two different times. In the third column, it reads 2225 when in the report on the fire, it says 1225. I'm just trying to find out --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Perhaps we can check the original, Your Honour. It may be a mistake or it may be a translation of somebody's mistake in the actual log.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you look at the previous entry, that's 130, it's more likely that it was 2225.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because the previous one is from 1825 which is confirmed in column six. I'll have a look at the original, if you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Munkelien, you understand the point I'm making. It seems at least from this document, that there were genuine attempts that were being made to put out fires in certain places; yes?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As you said, in certain places. Two of them occurred close to and one inside Sector South, so definitely -- but compared to all the fires that we observed, and if you are looking through our sitreps, you have now showed me four incidents where they have tried. I have 400 and even more that they didn't try. So I mean I still stand on my things in my report of 8 or 10 January 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many fire engines were there in Knin?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Fire engines.

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It was not a well-equipped fire service --

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- from what you could see at the time?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the Croatian authorities actually, to be fair about it, had severe limitations in what they could do in terms of their equipment, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It calls for a conclusion, Mr. Cayley. At the same time, Mr. Russo, if you are poorly-equipped even without putting a question, it would limit your possibilities, isn't that true? And limiting possibilities, of course, would be a conclusion but not a conclusion that could not be followed by anyone who uses his intellect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I make a comment? I mean I think Mr. Munkelien did acknowledge that the fire service was not well-equipped.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So I don't think -- it's not an unreasonable question to put to somebody that upon that basis, there would have been difficulties in actually trying to put out all of these fires. I don't think that that is an unreasonable question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not an unreasonable question, it's even an unnecessary question, I mean, if you are limited in your equipment. Either you explore how many there were and the witness doesn't know and then you go into details or you say they were limited in their equipment which the Chamber understands to limit their possibilities anyhow so --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could please look at D94.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Munkelien, this is a document that you were shown by my colleague Mr. Kehoe earlier and it's the document that refers to you being arrested at a checkpoint. Do you recall that document?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I'm actually interested in the second page. Now, just to confirm -- I don't want to go through this in detail, but it's fair to say that what is being reported here is observations on military matters, on force sizes, observation of armoured vehicles, troop movements, is that right, on this page?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very true.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we could please take a look at D28 once again, please. Now, after the fall of Knin, after the end of Operation Storm, the principal function of the UNMOs was to be involved in the observation of violations of international humanitarian law, recording burning houses, murdered individuals. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to this one, the effects of the hostilities and so on is mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we can go, please, to the next page and we looked at this before. Now, looking at paragraph 5 again, you were allowed to carry out surveillance in all areas -- and I'll read it so that I don't misquote it, " ... where, in the opinion of the local UNCRO military commander after consulting Croatian army commanders," the security situation permitted you to carry out that kind of surveillance. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this provision of the agreement concerns the observation and recording of humanitarian violations, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Say again the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This particular provision, this permission for observation and freedom of movement is directly linked to your role in observing and recording violations of humanitarian law, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it like that. I think that we had a role, freedom of movement and we should report in addition to troop movements and so on, we should report these humanitarian things as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But your role in actually reporting troop movements and military matters ended when Knin fell. Your role after that time was exclusively to report on humanitarian violations, wasn't it, officially, the official role according to this agreement?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you see, we reported it in, and I think even it was taken by Sector South headquarter and sent to Zagreb as well even the military things. We reported the humanitarian things, but we also reported the military things and that was taken into the report. I'm not sure if I've seen any of the reports from Sector South taking in the one that you showed me, but I think they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But to get an answer to my question, this agreement only envisages you reporting on human rights violations, doesn't it? You read the preamble just a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I can't say that this one only limits us to do the humanitarian things. We still had the task of reporting military movements as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you don't know really whether or not you had a legal right or an agreed right with the Croatian government to go on observing. If you don't know, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because we still continued on doing the same task as we had, military movements, military troops and then in addition we got this humanitarian task.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move on to another topic, and we're coming to the end now. This concerns, Mr. Munkelien, the 9 ARSK soldiers from Musica Stanovi. Do you remember that episode --

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- the arrest of those nine soldiers? Now, if you could look, please, at your second statement, the 2008 statement, and if you could go please to paragraph 33 and do you see there -- do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That you were present on the 29th of August in the village of Musica Stanovi when, "We met with local residents and 9 Serbian soldiers who had been hiding in the woods. We left the village and then met with some Croatian Special Police who were on their way to the village. We went back to the village with the special police, where the Serbian soldiers were handed over after we had obtained some guarantee of their safety. This incident is recorded in the document on the pages numbered 0038-7849 to 0038-7850. I can authenticate the record." Now, the question I have for you is this: Do you recall that this event actually took place over two days, that it actually started on the 28th of August and it ended on the 29th of August? From your own memory.

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I know it was a period of time, and everything didn't happen on the first day, so it must be 28th and the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But to the best of your recollection, you were actually there on the 29th of August?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there on the 29th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Okay. If please we could have 2D00-0017.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this document, Mr. Munkelien, just so you know what it is, it's actually a document that comes from the Prosecutor's office and it's a report, we believe, by UNCRO about this particular event. You'll see if it to be blown up, please. And you'll see that the date time group 29 August, 11.00, place, Musica Stanovi, UN present Lieutenant-Commander Alfonso, Major Komper and Major Tschernetsky all from UNMO Team Podkonje and then it lists the fact that Colonel Vaselko [phoen] from the command -- the commander of the special police unit, was also there and then it lists the names of those individuals. Now, what is somewhat puzzling for me is that your name is not actually listed on this document as being present. Is it possible that you were there the day before on the 28th of August?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I reported it being, like I said yesterday, an indoor man, that means running the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you were not there --

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- you think you may have actually received this report from the UNMO team that was on the ground, that you received a radio communication?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It may come to my memory that I was not present, but did the radio thing on it, on that date. Or we may have been two patrols on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So just to clarify your statement, it may well be the case that you in fact were not present at Musica Stanovi --

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- on the 29th?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, these individuals, are you aware that there were five located on the first day, on the 28th of August, as your memory serves you, and that on the second day, on the 29th when the authorities went back to the village, there were nine soldiers in the village, nine ARSK soldiers; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I remember. It was some coming forwards the first day and then the rest the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, we could -- in fact, Your Honour, if that could be given an exhibit number, please, that prior document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tender that document into evidence, Mr. Registrar. That would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D98.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D98. Mr. Russo, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D98 admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now have document 65 ter 1307.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this next document, Mr. Munkelien, is a report by General Markac, in fact, reporting on this episode as it took place, and he's making a report on the 28th of August to the chief of the Main Staff, Cervenko. And in fact if we go over the page because it's quite a lengthy report and we're only really interested in one particular section. If you could magnify that, please. If you could go down to about halfway down the page. Yes. It begins, "In the settlement of Lazica Stanovi." Can we blow up the English version, please, Mr. Registrar. Thank you. Now, you'll see written here -- do you see where it says, "In the settlement of Lazica Stanovi," I know it is a slightly different name, but it actually is the same place because the names of the individuals that you will see at the bottom are actually the same as the names on the list that I have shown you, at least five of them are the same of the nine. So you will see there it refers about halfway down, "A member of the United Nations Alun Roberts spokesman from the former Sector South and another three military observers were found in one of the houses in the cited settlement. They were in the company of five enemy soldiers namely, Nenad Todorovic, member -- born in 1972, member of the 92nd Motorised Brigade, Benkovac; Milan Todorovic, born in 1966, a member of the military police since 1992, and a member of the 1st Brigade since 1993; Milan Mirkovic born in 1959, a member of the Golubic training centre, and it also mentions Juro Mirkovic and Stevo Mirkovic." Then the next sentence you read, "The listed persons were not immediately detained in the Knin police department due to the presence of Alun Roberts but it will be done tomorrow in the presence of the fundamental police unit of Knin Police Department." Then it refers to the weapons that were recovered nearby. Were you aware that, in fact, these individuals were not taken into civilian police custody until the 29th of August?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I know that because we -- I think we reported it to the headquarter and then Alun Roberts got the task to go there together with the UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So on the 29th of August, the UNMOs returned with Alun Roberts and the civilian police and took these individuals plus the other four?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was on the 28th, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, do you see that it states here, "The listed persons were not immediately detained in Knin Police Department due to the presence of Alun Roberts but it will be done tomorrow in the presence of the fundamental police unit of Knin Police Department." So the question I have for you is: Are you aware that the soldiers remained in the village that day?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were not actually taken into custody by the civilian police until the following day?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I know that. But I can't tell you if they were found on the 28th and taken into prison on the 29th or if they were found some days before and then taken in on the 29th because definitely they were taken in on the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. And they were taken eventually to the Knin school, to the collection centre that was being run at the school, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that. I know that we later picked up the -- those from the village and took them to the school, to the centre and later escorted them into the buses that went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the collection centre where these individuals were eventually taken, that, as far as you can recall, that was run by the civilian police; yes?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- I can't recall that, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Thank you. Yes, could that be given, please, an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D99.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D99 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I want to talk to you very briefly again, Mr. Munkelien, about checkpoints. Now, again, relying on your knowledge as a professional army officer, how many individuals, personnel, I'm talking about, do you need to operate a checkpoint if, say, you're working in three shifts?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ideally, you should have eight times -- no, yeah, normal shift, eight hours. That means three at a shift, 24 personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you need at least 24 personnel?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that should be the ideal if you are in peacetime and the regulation for working hours and so on. Otherwise, it could be done by two shifts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I try to follow the calculations? 24 hours a day --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- three shifts means one shift, eight hours. You said three at a shift.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you need three personnel at one shift.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That means nine, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means nine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do we agree that the 24, the proper calculation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Take it away, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm actually completely confused by the math now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what the witness did, as a matter of fact, he multiplied the number of personnel you need at a checkpoint by the number of hours --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a shift takes rather than by the number of shifts you need in one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think it's now corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And 24 has now been reduced to nine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And again with checkpoints, what kinds of equipment do you need to equip a checkpoint properly?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you need more than personnel standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm talking about equipment. You need radio communications?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, I think we've gone through that. You need maybe a car to come there. You need communication, maybe some cones to put up and some weapons and so on. And back to the figures, you could make it two men in 12-hour shift, that means four personnel as well. That reduces the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any further questions of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. The Markac Defence, Mr. Kuzmanovic or Mr. Mikulicic, who is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It will be me, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kuzmanovic, who is counsel for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Munkelien.

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There are a couple of themes I would like to go over with you similar to what Mr. Cayley did, not the same questions obviously but the same kind of methodology. Before you testified yesterday, have you had the occasion at all to speak with Mr. Anttila in the last six to eight months?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: When is the last time that you spoke with Mr. Anttila?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1995 during the period that we were in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you spoken to anyone else from the UNMOs before you came to testify at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a brief conversation with Peter Marti on the telephone from Norway to Sudan, just after I was done here 10th of January, this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Munkelien, you had given us a description of the UNMOs generally and of the kinds of vehicles you had and generally what your responsibilities were. Could you give us an indication of what your daily procedure was, how you would start your day, what you would do during the day, what you would come back to do in the evening?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you may be aware of, we were living in the same house and we had a garage where we had two cars parked. We had sharing bedrooms and one living-room that also served as the office for the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, let me interrupt you for a moment. Maybe my question was misunderstood. What I'm looking for is you'd get up, you'd go to the -- to your headquarters. What would you do? How would you get your assignments? How would you go on to the terrain? Who decided those things?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I was directly into that one, because then I said we were working from the bedroom and into the living-room and there we had our morning brief and from there on we got the tasks and said you and you go in that direction, you and you go in that direction. In the beginning, we were up to four in one patrol because we lacked vehicles, and latter it was normal to run two in each patrol. And then we reported on radio if something in particular happened back to the radioman that was in the living-room. And apart from that, we reported back in the afternoon and that was the sitrep that was given to Sector South. As by the afternoon, I can't recall the special timing, but I know during the day, we should report to Sector South and give our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So if you went on a patrol, for example, let's, for example, talk about a patrol that you went on in any patrol, you would get in your vehicle and you would take off for whatever area you would cover?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that would take all day?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could take all day, but it also could be that you went back, reported what you have seen in that area, and then continued in another direction. For example, going to Strmica, coming back, and then going up in another direction like south or westerly or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Now, the terrain that you patrolled was fairly mountainous, was it not?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And it was very wooded?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So it would provide good cover for people who were hiding out; would it not?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, it was -- you couldn't cover it all. As I said, we were using vehicles but also for the patrols, not in a big extent, but stopped at particular areas, and went in, talked with the people present and got information from them as well. Not only the thing that we observed ourself but also firsthand from the remaining population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You understood, did you not, that the Croatian Special Police in August were conducting mop-up operations in various parts of Sector South; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I know they were doing some of this one in the area. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you described one of those incidences in regard to the handover of the Serbian soldiers on the 29th of August, did you not? That was the result of a mop-up operation, was it not?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm not sure if it was a mop-up or if we reported it and they came to mop it up afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You are familiar with Mr. Tschernetsky, are you not?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tschernetsky was a UNMO?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the deputy UNMO Knin and later became the team leader of Team Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Tschernetsky was from Russia, correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was from Russia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic and you, Mr. Munkelien, you are developing a speed of speech which causes problems for the interpreter and the transcriber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, the name on page 62 -- on 32, 43, Tschernetsky. I think that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Names are usually corrected --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just for the benefit, I'll spell it for -- it's T-s-c-h-e-r-n-e-t-s-k-y.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When reference is made to pages, I noted that the pages on the screen we cannot manipulate is different from the pages on our screen with the e-court screen with the LiveNote on it so therefore, references, usually it's one page difference. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Munkelien, are you aware that the arrest of these Serbian ARSK soldiers on August 29th was proceeded earlier that week by a visit from Mr. Tschernetsky to these same soldiers?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I heard a story about that, that they had discovered these RSK soldiers up in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that Mr. Tschernetsky did not decide to report these soldiers but instead gave them maps to try to get to Bosnia, did he not?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that because all the things that we discovered was reported. I can't say that on that and that day, that was reported to the higher headquarter but I'm sure he did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean you're sure that he gave a map to the soldiers for them to try to get to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. I'm sure that he reported to the higher headquarter what he had found on his patrol up to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Was it within your mandate to give maps to soldiers of the ARSK to try to get them out of the area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, I think the witness said that he's not aware of that. What's the use of asking him whether that was within his mandate?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's just a general question, Your Honour, not specific to this, but to any ARSK soldier that they may have found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You could put 100 questions in that respect. It continues or it relies, more or less, on rumours. I mean that makes the whole relevance of this, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, sure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is no occasion of providing maps, then the occasion becomes rather irrelevant, because you could ask all kind of things, is it -- was distributing all kind of stuff within the mandate. Of course we would not expect that it would be in the mandate unless there's any reason to assume that it happened or that for one reason or another that it's a reasonable assumption that other people considered it to be within the mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it, Mr. Munkelien, if I'm -- if you would not have answered that question, I would not have thought that this was within your mandate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I totally agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So it would, for example, it would not be normal procedure for someone upon coming upon an ARSK soldier to give them a map to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please move on, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I just answer that by saying we were not neutral, but we were totally impartial. We didn't help any of the parties in any way that you are indicating in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that any -- if any of the HV Special Police -- strike that. Are you aware of any of the former ARSK soldiers that were arrested on the 29th of August and brought to Knin, are you aware if any of those people were brought up on any criminal charges?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would the usher please -- or the registrar please call up 3D00-0080 up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Munkelien, I'll represent to you that one of the persons on the list of soldiers previously identified as Milan Mirkovic was brought up on criminal charges in this particular document. Do you see that on the left?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I see that. It's dated 6 June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I get an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D100.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kuzmanovic, just in order to see whether we have the same understanding of certain terms, you said "was brought up on criminal charges." May I take it that from this document, it does not appear that he was charged but that a criminal report was drafted and sent by the police to the military Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will be more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move this exhibit into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D100 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to refer back, now, Mr. Munkelien, to the D49, if the registrar could bring that up, please, page 2. Now, my colleague Mr. Cayley was asking you some questions about this document, that's the order from the Ministry of the Interior, Mr. Maric to the local police stations and police administration to take specific steps to prevent further activity; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you yourself said that prevention was the first step in trying to prevent criminal activity such as what was going on from was happening; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that at least as -- that the intent of this particular document was precisely that, to prevent continued disorder from occurring?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that this looks very well on paper, but when it comes to the land, it was hard to have it into action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to talk to you a bit about a restriction of movement. You, yourself, said during your testimony that you and I would presume other UNMOs when out on patrol were able to get around checkpoints; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean if we were stopped, we didn't go too much into the terrain due to the -- maybe the danger of mines and so on, but on this particular occasion that we talked about, it was with a consensus of the higher headquarter that we went about and came behind the mountains in Strmica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Mr. Munkelien, that if you were able to circumvent a checkpoint, people who were intent on looting and burning could do the same thing?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not normally, because they were having normal cars. We had all four-wheel drives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It would be possible, would it not?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is possible if you have the intent and the wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the looting that you observed taking place, Mr. Munkelien, I note that you had earlier stated that there were no photographs that you personally took of any of this activity that was going on; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you took no photographs of any of the torching that was going on; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There were photographs, however, that were taken of the people who were shot or murdered; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, like the one that was shown today or we discussed yesterday on the Babic case. That was done by the headquarter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any particular reason why the UNMOs didn't have even a Polaroid camera or something to take photographs of their observations?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been thinking about it now that maybe should have more -- the digital camera wasn't at that time, but Polaroid was definitely there. We didn't use it to document anything so -- of this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The specific acts of looting that you talked about or in general you talked about looting, what do you determine or how do you determine whether a house has been looted? Do you go inside of it? Do you conduct an internal investigation in the home? Could you explain to us how you determine something was looted?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally, you saw it from outside that something had happened, but you also went a little bit inside and saw that, okay, somebody's been there and dragged out things and maybe put -- if it was running water, put the tap on, so definitely the floor was ruined or you saw that the doors, the window frames, like I also have described, was taken away. So you could see it both on the inside when you went in or you could, in some cases, see it from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you saw it from the outside, what would you have seen from the outside?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That normally things were dragged out and maybe left outside the house. They couldn't carry it or it was of no interest but they had taken it out from the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You have noted a few occasions that you saw people actually engaging in that kind of conduct; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to state that the vast majority of the time that you determined something was looted, it was simply by observation, meaning that you didn't see anybody in the act of looting?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw people in the act of looting. But as you said, I can't document this one on -- other than the reports that we gave in, I have no photos and the memory may be a bad thing, but at least the reports that we gave in gave the evidence that it did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, were these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Munkelien, apparently you misunderstood the question that you had not seen people in the act of looting. The question was whether it's fair to say that in the vast majority of the cases of looting, that you didn't see anyone in the act of looting. So I think Mr. Kuzmanovic wanted to know what approximately was the proportion of cases where you did see people in the act of looting and whether, in the vast majority, you did not see people in the act of looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. 10 per cent of all the looting that we reported, maybe less, was directly observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The same thing with the burning of homes. Can you describe for us what percentage in your observations of the burning of homes that you saw were homes that were actually set on fire by someone as opposed to a house that you saw burning?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have one example in my statements that I saw it directly and the rest is observing houses burning for some reason or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Active burning, actual --

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Active ignition, I didn't see they did it, because they went into the house and then when they came out again, the house started to burn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear, that's the instance that you saw someone actually burning a home?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the rest of the time you would either see that the home was burning itself but there was no one else around it?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now when -- did you make any attempt to -- strike the question. Before you came to Sector South, did you have any understanding as to what damage was caused to homes and buildings in the area before Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So is it fair to state that at least as far as you're concerned, you could not differentiate between anything that may have been burned or destroyed before Operation Storm compared to after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Myself, I couldn't separate that one, but as you see in the report from Kari Anttila, he said at least in one occasion, ruined before Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. But you yourself could not make that distinction?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I could not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I try to further explore that, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you say you cannot make a distinction. Now I can imagine that whether it was before Operation Storm, let's say the 25th of July compared to the 10th of August that it would be difficult to make any distinction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the other hand, if a house would have been burned three, four, five years earlier, would you still consider that you could make no distinction if you observe a house which was burned a long -- couple of years before --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or more recently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Then you could see it because then the trees were growing up again around it and you couldn't -- you could distinct them between those from former times and this that happened now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you're telling, therefore, where you earlier said that you could not distinguish between houses burnt before or during Operation Storm, that you now are telling that under certain circumstances, you could see that a house was burned considerable time before you observed it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I could observe that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Munkelien, can you tell us, if you know, the difference between buildings that were damaged from active combat operations during Operation Storm and -- I'll strike the question. It's a confusing question. Can you tell us, please, whether you could detect among your patrols what buildings were either burned or destroyed as a result of combat operations during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally, if you are talking about destroyed by shelling, you could normally see the impact of mortar or rocket and then see it out from that. But normally, when it was the -- the building was fired on, you could see broken tiles and you could see scars in the wood in the walls making -- coming from automatic weapons or something. So you could do some distinction, but of course normally, you said that, yes, it's destroyed by -- during the Operation Storm because people had been there before and they knew what houses had not been destroyed before that. The team was not new in Knin, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. I guess my question is that there were -- I guess there were three categories of destruction here; were there not? There was what was damaged before Operation Storm --

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- or burned, what was damaged during the operation, during combat operations of Operation Storm; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And there was what was damaged or burned after Operation Storm that had nothing to do with combat operations?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And is it fair to state that your reports on burning and destruction of property don't distinguish between those three categories?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the report that we gave in on the 17th was the report directly on the area or all Sector South reports was on direct result of Operation Storm. And then from then on, it was a little bit increasing on that one on the 20th, then the 21st, but from then on, it was houses that was looted, damaged, burned by other -- or later than Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to go into of any of the hamlets away from the road to determine whether homes were burned on looted?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we covered most of the hamlets in the whole area to specifically look for people and then we also observed the building and reported on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that given the remote location of some of these hamlets and villages, that it would be relatively easy for someone who wanted to to go out and loot?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean that we couldn't see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I think we covered most of -- I've been climbing a lot in the area, so I think I've seen most of the passes and roads that was not used by cars. So I think we covered most of the distant hamlets in the area as well as along the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I guess in conjunction with that question, Mr. Munkelien, a lot of these villages and hamlets you agreed with me were fairly remote, difficult to get to, were they not?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And it wouldn't be very easy to detect or prevent someone who was very intent on looting to get to those hamlets and villages to do that?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but now we are talking about looting of heavily things, so I mean you don't go carrying a lot of things from a house that was only had a path, you were using normally a car to have access to the house, and then you loot it and then you took whatever you needed, left the rest behind, and then went away with the car. You didn't go on remote areas without the possibility to drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: But it did happen in those remote areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did happen as well, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And it went undetected, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I'd like to clarify when he says "it did happen" if he's referring to it, looting with a car or it, looting without a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Looting, period, with or without a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's fine, Judge, I just wanted that to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looting that happened in remote hamlets. Yes. So there we are. Looting happened and it remained undetected, you said, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it could be undetected at the time, but during the period we were there, I think we covered most of the hamlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And what I mean by "undetected," meaning it could be also undetected by the civil police; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, if it was not reported by us or somebody else, it was -- it could go undetected, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, earlier a distinction was made between observing the act of looting and observing looted houses, that is, not seen someone looting it. If we are talking about detection, it might be useful to make a similar distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Munkelien, it's fair to state that at least as far as looting is concerned, it's true, is it not, that the looters were able to evade, to a certain extent, the civil police; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I said, normally, the looting was done by people in cars. That means if they kept on the road, they could be stopped at the checkpoints. If they had a -- knew any bypasses, of course, they could manage to trick the checkpoints, but I think that was not - what shall I say - done in the most cases. The most cases were done by people in cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to take a look, and I'd like to ask the usher to pull up and I believe this is the map but I'm not certain. P70 is the map that Mr. Munkelien drew on, I'm not sure if that -- or P62, I'm sorry. Is that the one that the witness drew on?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe that is P70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P70, with seven markings on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Munkelien, I'd like to direct your attention to the areas that you've marked PA.

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: PA were the sections that you stated that you investigated before the provisional assessment of damage was made on August 18th of 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are putting the word "investigation" make it very seriously. I say more patrolling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. What would you have done when you conducted that patrol, just driven through the area and taken a look to see what was damaged?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Driving around, stopping and then counting buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were others assigned to your detachment driving in other parts of Knin to do the same thing?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at that time, we were two teams out, so yes, there may be others covering other areas at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if it's possible, if we could put the map -- we'll come back to the map in a minute, I'd like to pull up P64, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you could take a look at paragraph 1. I'll read the second sentence of paragraph 1. "The report is based on a rundown of 70 per cent of Knin town and gives only a brief overview of the situation." Now, obviously the section that you looked at was not 70 per cent of Knin town; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So is it fair to state that others in your unit were able to cover the remainder of Knin town to make it the equivalent of 70 per cent to make this assessment possible?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, or maybe 70 per cent is a little bit high.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the report says 70 per cent; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Point 2 of the report says, in the last sentence, "Only few, three to five impacts is observed in other urban areas." Now, given the fact that 70 per cent of the town was assessed preliminarily, the report concludes three to five impacts observed in other urban areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to go to page 2 of that document now, please. Paragraph 6. I'm reading the second sentence. "Especially para 2 is considered sensitive and must not be released to the media at the present stage. This information should therefore be kept confidential for internal use only." Mr. Munkelien, was there any particular reason that you were aware of why the media was not to be told that the shelling was concentrated against military objectives discussed in paragraph 2 of this report?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. And as you see, it's the senior military observer who have done this report so I had no influence except from giving him the data that he reported in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any political pressure that you were aware of being put on the military observers not to release this information?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know or there was none?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to get back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, let's try to understand that last answer. The question was, "Was there any political pressure that you were aware of being put on the military observers not to release this information?" You were a military observer, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a military observer, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And your answer was no. And the question was you don't know or there was none. "I don't know." The question was in general about military observers. You were one of them. So we have two options: For others, whether you knew about it, and for yourself, whether you were ever put under any pressure. Could you first answer the question in relation to yourself, was there any political pressure upon you when reporting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no political pressure on me on reporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And were you aware of any of the other military observers, either at your level or at any other level that were under such pressure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no others were under pressure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the commander of Sector South was under any political pressure from anyone not to release this information?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware that he was under any pressure to -- not to release it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And I think you told us already, you don't know why this was not released to the media; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to the issue of the looting for a moment. You had stated in answer to some of my questions or to one of the questions that it was difficult for many of the vehicles to get into these hamlets because they didn't have four-wheel drive like your vehicles did; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that for the most part, the -- your observations of the looting took place with people using civilian vehicles?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian and in some cases also military vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you -- the percentage of people using civilian vehicles were the vast majority, were they not?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilians -- the civilian vehicles were the majority, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Munkelien [sic], I'd like you to call up D91, please. This is the September 4th, 1999 statement. The third page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The first full paragraph, Mr. Munkelien, starts, "I cannot remember any single episode when I saw any burning while patrolling the area. I saw some burning in Knin." Did I read that correctly?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I see the statement is there, but according to my reports, I saw a lot of burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You signed the statement in April of -- it appears to be September 4th of 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And at least as of September 4th, 1999 when you saw this statement, when you signed this statement that you read -- I presume that you read it before signing it; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You could not remember any single episode when you saw any burning while patrolling?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I read the sentence, but compared to our reports, it doesn't make any sense now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Russo, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If you could please look, Mr. Munkelien, at your second statement. I believe that's P61. If you could please direct your attention to paragraph 38. If you could please review paragraph 38 and perhaps explain to the Court the statement that was just reviewed with you by Mr. Kuzmanovic regarding whether or not you could recall seeing any incidents of burning or looting.

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I corrected that one now this year because as you have read in our reports, the daily sitreps, we made a lot of reports on burning houses during my period in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked by Mr. Cayley first, and then by Mr. Kuzmanovic, questions regarding an order by Joska Moric and that was Defence Exhibit D49 if we could please call that up. If you recall, this was the document that was shown to you and you were asked the number of hypothetical questions about what could have been done, what should have been done to prevent looting and burning. You were asked to take a look at this document and I believe -- I'm not sure if it was discussed during that examination but I believe it did indicate that crimes which had occurred prior to the date of this order would not be investigated. Is that your understanding of the document as well? If we could turn to perhaps the second page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, that is what the document says. That's what we heard previous evidence. That's what we heard was read to this witness. So is there any reason to again verify that it is the gist of this document on this specific point?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: There is no reason, Your Honour, I'm move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you could have refrained from it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Asking questions to you with regard to what could have been done and I think the point was made that it took some time to get this order up and running and to actually effectuate the order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And based on your recollection, can you recall whether or not after or sometime even weeks after the 18th of August when this order was issued, whether or not the crimes referenced in there continued to happen?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It continued to happen a lot of crimes but of course the police were also more present, especially in Knin town. We saw them very seldom out in the remote areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And from your recollection of reviewing the sitreps, did you report the continuing commission of these offences in those sitreps?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We reported whatever we observed in our sitreps, the daily sitreps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, in line with what we discussed earlier we would like to move into evidence across the bar table the sitreps which indicate from this date forward the crimes which were catalogued. We can do that once the witness leaves just to help time purposes if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, overloading the Chamber with reports covering all different kind of subjects might not be a very good idea. If -- we have seen already that in Exhibits 67 there are some nice colours in it. I don't know who coloured. We find green, we find all kind of different markings on it. Just saying, "Trial Chamber, here are 60 sitreps, do what you want with it" is not the appropriate way of proceeding. The -- if there are certain matters for which you want to present these sitreps to the Trial Chamber, please explain briefly what you are drawing our attention to and then seek it to be admitted and then we'll hear from the Defence whether there are any objections to that so that we have a focused view on bulky material which we receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll certainly do that and we're prepared to indicate with respect to each document the information contained in the document which we would direct the Court's attention to but we can do that at another time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Munkelien, if you also recall during I believe it was Mr. Cayley's questioning, there was a discussion about efforts that were made to put some fires out and I believe Mr. Cayley said -- asked you to agree and I believe you did agree that the Croatian authorities had severe limitations in what they could do in terms of their equipment and I think you agreed with that; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please pull up 65 ter number 2367, and it is a lengthy document and I would simply ask you to move to page 89, please, of the English translation. I believe that is page 55 of the B/C/S translation, just to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If you could look at your screen on the entry, if we could highlight the entry for 0620. As you can see here, this is a report indicating around the 9th or 10th of August, 1995, in the OG Sibenik that a report concerning a fire in the area, this is between the villages of Biocic and Miocic that "cannons were in danger and that they engaged fire fighting planes and the fire was put out." Did I read that correctly? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's fire fighting plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, only one plane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that makes it safer as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Do you know where the villages of Biocic and Miocic are?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not directly, because it refers to Sibenik, so I can't -- I have to see a map and some grid references to -- I can't tell you. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you ever see any aircraft being engaged to put any of the fires out that you or your UNMOs happened to come upon?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender this document into evidence, this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this the part of the police -- it is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not yet offered into evidence. It is a part of the operational diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, then I am mistaken. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he doesn't know where it is, I don't understand how the document can even come into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, why not? Do you have to know exactly what place it is. I think Mr. Russo is focussing on the availability and the use of a plane for fire-fighting in the area covered by this document. But if you say this is not Sector South, it's not even near to Knin -- and we know that planes fly far faster than firefighters can drive - then please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'd only make the point, Your Honour, that Sibenik is not in Knin, Sibenik is on the coast, it's far away from Knin city which is specifically what I was following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it within the -- as I said, planes go far faster. Sibenik is at what distance from Knin? And I'm not asking -- I take it that you can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's some confusion. The reference in the diary is to OG Sibenik, that is the operational group Sibenik. The military group which had responsibility for this area, where it occurred were the villages of Biocic and Miocic, which is in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think -- you say -- I do not know exactly where these villages are but it is within Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Kuzmanovic, your objection was based on that Mr. Russo didn't know where it was. He now tells us that it is in Sector South. Does your objection stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think the whole purpose of using a plane is put out a fire is to put out a fire in a rural wooded area. I mean I think it's impractical, it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It goes without --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- about houses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But is that a matter of admissibility or a matter of weight to be given to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think since he doesn't really know where this is, Your Honour, I don't know how it's admissible if he doesn't even know where this place is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is clear, that at least once, a plane was used for the purpose of extinguishing a fire in an area, because that's what it says, in Sector South, not more, not less. That is mainly relevant for the availability of at least that plane at that moment. Objection denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could have an exhibit number for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this becomes Exhibit P71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P71 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My only -- my last issue, Your Honour, is not necessarily a question for the witness. It's with respect to a document which was shown to the witness during the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you put a question in relation to a document in the presence of a witness you should always be very careful not by just putting the question, drawing the attention of a witness to a certain element of that document that could trigger further comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know what you want to draw -- what you wanted to ask but please keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE GOTOVINA DEFENCE
utterances.text: Mr. Munkelien, if you can recall yesterday when you were being

utterances.speaker: THE GOTOVINA DEFENCE
utterances.text: was marked for identification as D89. If we could bring that up, please. You recall discussing this document in the context of artillery fire coming from the side of the ARSK towards Knin in the direction north north-east of Knin?

utterances.speaker: TOR MUNKELIEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe this document was tendered into evidence. I would move at this point to have the entire document entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do believe that I did put it into evidence. If I didn't under the D number, it was simply an oversight on my part but I did intend to put it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, our records indicate that it was only marked for identification and it was never admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it was marked for identification under what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Under D89, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D89. No objection. Therefore it is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Bench has no further questions for you, Mr. Munkelien. Therefore, this concludes your evidence. I would like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague, of having answered the questions by the parties, and by the Bench and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Munkelien out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break and then after the break, I take it that the Prosecution will call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, before we take the break, I'd like to address a certain matter, and Mr. Cayley, you are the -- well, not to say the victim of it, but ... For this witness, this witness said something about extinguishing fires and sending fire brigades. Now that led to taking us through this police log where of course the witness couldn't say anything apart from that at least some activity undertaken as a result of fire was there.
